prompt: In a new terminal, `az storage container list` asks which account to use, while the old terminal still works. What was skipped?
hint: Which of the three lines tells the command line where storage is?

choices.text: Starting Azurite again, which stopped between the two terminals
choices.why: The old terminal still works, so Azurite is up; a stopped one gives a refused connection.

choices.text: Exporting the connection string
choices.why: Right. Without it the command line has no account to talk to, and says so.

choices.text: Signing in with az login, which storage commands need first
choices.why: Storage commands with a connection string need no sign-in; az login is for Resource Manager.

choices.text: Activating the virtual environment in the second terminal
choices.why: Then `az` itself would not be found, and nothing would ask about an account.

prompt: `az storage container list` fails with a message that the API version is not supported by Azurite. What do you do?
hint: Which of the two programs is out of date?

choices.text: Start Azurite with the option that skips the version check
choices.why: That makes the two programs disagree in silence instead of loudly.

choices.text: Install an older Azure command line
choices.why: It would work, and leaves you on a version none of the lessons uses.

choices.text: Remove the container and start the pinned Azurite image
choices.why: Right. The old image is the stale half; the pinned one speaks the API version the command line sends.

choices.text: Export the connection string again
choices.why: The request reached Azurite, which is why Azurite could refuse it.

prompt: `az group list` answers `Please run 'az login' to setup account.` in the lab. What does that tell you?

choices.text: Azurite needs a password before it can list resource groups
choices.why: Azurite emulates storage only; it has no resource groups to list.

choices.text: The connection string points at the wrong storage account
choices.why: The connection string is for storage commands; `az group` never reads it.

choices.text: Resource Manager is not in the lab
choices.why: Right. Resource groups belong to it, and nothing on your computer imitates it.

choices.text: The region was not set
choices.why: A region is chosen per resource; the refusal comes before any region matters.

prompt: Which of these does this course run on your computer? Choose all that apply.
hint: Compiling, checking and querying, yes; anything Resource Manager decides, no.

choices.text: Compiling a Bicep file to an ARM template
choices.why: Yes. `bicep build` runs locally and needs no subscription.

choices.text: Swapping an App Service slot
choices.why: No. A swap is a Resource Manager operation; lesson 3 teaches it from the documentation.

choices.text: A KQL query over a table you loaded
choices.why: Yes. The Kusto emulator runs the query language itself.

choices.text: A log alert firing and sending an e-mail
choices.why: No. You evaluate the alert's query yourself; nothing fires.

choices.text: Taking a lease on a blob, the way Terraform locks its state
choices.why: Yes. Azurite implements leases, and lesson 6 uses one.

prompt: A Bicep file for a key vault compiles cleanly with `bicep build`. Your colleague concludes it will deploy. What is the flaw?

choices.text: None: a clean compile means Azure will accept the deployment
choices.why: Compiling checks form; names already taken, quotas and your own permissions are checked by Azure.

choices.text: It proves form, not what Azure would allow
choices.why: Right. A vault name taken worldwide, a policy that denies it, a role you lack: all are refused at deployment.

choices.text: Bicep has no type for key vaults
choices.why: It can; every Resource Manager type is describable in Bicep.

choices.text: It also needs `terraform validate`
choices.why: Terraform does not read Bicep; the two are separate tools.

prompt: Match each level of a pipeline to what it is.
hint: Only one of them gets a machine.

pairs.right: A named phase that runs after the ones it depends on
The unit sent to an agent, with its own fresh machine
One script or task, run in order on its job's agent

prompt: A job builds `dist/app.zip`. The next job, in the same stage, cannot find it. Why?

choices.text: Jobs in one stage share a disk, so the path must be wrong
choices.why: They share nothing; each job gets its own agent.

choices.text: Each job has its own machine
choices.why: Right. Only an artifact, published and downloaded again, crosses from one job to another.

choices.text: The second job ran first, since jobs in a stage run in parallel
choices.why: Order matters when jobs depend on each other, and still no file would cross without an artifact.

choices.text: Files under dist/ are deleted at the end of every step
choices.why: Steps of one job share its agent and its disk.

prompt: A pull request triggers the shop's pipeline. Which stages run?

choices.text: Both, because the trigger includes the main branch
choices.why: The trigger decides whether the run starts, not which stages it keeps.

choices.text: Build only; Deploy's condition is false
choices.why: Right. The condition requires refs/heads/main, so a pull request is built and tested and deploys nothing.

choices.text: Deploy only, with the image of the last main build
choices.why: Deploy depends on Build and never runs without it.

choices.text: Neither of them
choices.why: Builds of pull requests are common, and are what keeps main green.

prompt: The step `azureSubscription: shop-production` names a service ___, an object holding how to sign in to Azure.
hint: One word, the second half of the object's name.

prompt: A template decides whether to include a stage with `${{ if eq(variables['deployNow'], 'yes') }}`, and `deployNow` is set by a script step during the run. What happens?
hint: When is a template expression resolved?

choices.text: It is never included: the expression is resolved before any step runs
choices.why: Right. Template expressions see only what exists at compile time; a value set at run time comes too late.

choices.text: It is included as soon as the script step sets the variable during the run
choices.why: The list of stages is fixed before the first agent starts.

choices.text: The pipeline fails to compile
choices.why: It compiles; the variable is simply absent at that moment, and the condition is false.

choices.text: It works if written as $(deployNow) instead
choices.why: A macro is filled in at run time, inside a step; it cannot decide whether a stage exists.

prompt: What makes `extends` stronger than including a template with `- template:`?

choices.text: Extended templates run faster on Microsoft-hosted agents
choices.why: Speed is the same; the difference is who controls the frame.

choices.text: Only `extends` accepts parameters at all
choices.why: Included templates take parameters too, as the test template in this lesson does.

choices.text: An environment check enforces it
choices.why: Right. An include can be deleted by the team; a required-template check refuses a deployment that does not extend it.

choices.text: It copies the template into the repository, so nobody else changes it
choices.why: It references the other repository; the tag is what keeps it from moving.

prompt: A canary deployment job runs with `increments: [10, 50]`. Who moves 10% of the traffic to the new version?
hint: What does the strategy actually do at each increment?

choices.text: Azure Pipelines, through the agent
choices.why: The pipeline only calls your steps with the increment; it moves nothing.

choices.text: Your own steps, through whatever receives the traffic
choices.why: Right. The hooks are places for steps, and the steps ask the platform, such as App Service, to move it.

choices.text: The environment object, which routes requests
choices.why: An environment records deployments and holds checks; it routes nothing.

choices.text: Azure Front Door, automatically, when it sees a canary job
choices.why: Nothing outside reacts to a job's strategy unless your steps tell it to.

prompt: The environment's history shows last night's deployment in green, and customers report errors since then. What does that history prove?

choices.text: That the new version is healthy, so the errors come from elsewhere
choices.why: Green means the steps exited without error, not that the application works.

choices.text: That the deployment never actually happened
choices.why: It happened; the history is the record that it did.

choices.text: Which run and commit reached production, and when
choices.why: Right. It answers what changed and when, which is where the investigation starts; whether it works is for the application's own signals.

choices.text: That an approval step was skipped somewhere along the way
choices.why: Nothing in the history says so; approvals are checks, recorded separately when they exist.

prompt: Put what happens to a commit on main in the shop's pipeline in order.
hint: Compile before agents, test before push, deploy last.
items: The YAML at that commit is compiled, templates included
An agent runs Install and Test
The image is built and pushed, tagged with the commit
trap: Thinking the agents start first is the slip: the list of stages and steps exists before any machine does.

prompt: Three teams copy the same test setup into their pipelines, and the platform team wants a dependency scan to run before every deployment to production. What do you build?
hint: One part is for convenience and one for enforcement.

choices.text: A steps template the teams include, and nothing else
choices.why: It removes the copies and enforces nothing: a team can delete the include.

choices.text: A wiki page listing the required steps
choices.why: Documentation is read on the days somebody remembers it.

choices.text: A separate pipeline that scans every repository at night
choices.why: It reports after the fact; a deployment could reach production first.

choices.text: An `extends` template, and a required-template check on shop-production
choices.why: Right. The template removes the copies, and the check refuses a deployment that does not extend it.

prompt: A pipeline has two stages. Build holds two jobs that run in parallel; Deploy holds one deployment job and one smoke-test job. How many agents does one full run use, counting each job's machine once?
